newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: SOCCER-ZIMBABWE CONFIDENT OF CUP QUALIFICATION AT LAST.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ZIMBABWE CONFIDENT OF CUP QUALIFICATION AT LAST.

text.p: Zimbabwe are finally confident of winning an elusive place in the African Nations Cup finals after nearly two decades of heartbreak.
The southern African country have never qualified for the biannual African championship and have built up an unenviable reputation for failing at the final hurdle.
But a 1-0 win over Angola at the weekend has put them within two points of qualification for the 1998 tournament, to be held in Burkina Faso next February.
A disputed penalty by South African-based striker Wilfred Mugeyi gave the Zimbabweans a vital victory in group one of the qualifiers in Harare on Sunday and joint top place in the group with Ghana.

Both sides have four points while Angola have yet to get off the mark and with two matches left for each country, Zimbabwe have a very real chance of going through to their first finals. One team qualifies from the group.

"I think we've got a very good chance this time round. We really just need one or two more points to make 100 percent sure," says the team's Scottish coach Ian Porterfield, an English F.A. Cup winner as a player who then went on to manage several British clubs.
Zimbabwe's past qualifying record is a tale of woe with the country squandering gilt-edged chances of making it to the Nations Cup finals.
Two years ago they lost out on a trip to the finals in South Africa when key players refused to travel to Zaire at the height of the Ebola virus crisis and the side lost 5-0.

For the finals in Tunisia in 1994, Zimbabwe had to beat neighbours Zambia at home in the last game but conceded a goal 10 minutes from time to draw. It was the same story for the 1992 finals in Senegal, when a injury-time equaliser put Congo through instead of Zimbabwe.
Ten years ago, unfancied Kenya edged them out on the away goals rule in the qualifiers in another surprise reversal.

But Porterfield, who was in charge of Zambia when they were runners-up in Tunisia in 1994, believes he has the right mix to get the country through to the finals next year despite supporters' scepticism.
He has disregarded public opinion by picking a youthful side with several new additions since taking over in November.

"We've been doing very well since I came here but there are very many negative people in this country. The team have done really, really well but all the young lads have got is criticism. Where are (the fans') heroes? What have they achieved in the past?"
Zimbabwe travel to Ghana in July for their next Nations Cup qualifier and then face a return match against Angola two weeks later to decide their fate.
"If we had drawn with these guys we would have been out," goalscorer Mugeyi said after Sunday's match. "But now we can qualify."
"Of course, we are back in the race," said Kennedy Chihuri, who plays for Slavia Prague in the Czech Republic and is among a growing number of his compatriots playing in Europe.
Factors standing in the way of Zimbabwe's progress remain uncertainly over Porterfield's tenure and the future of English-based players Bruce Grobbelaar and Peter Ndlovu.
Porterfield contract runs out in April and he is not sure whether he will stay. "My family are not here so that's always very hard," he said.

Goalkeeper Grobbelaar, who has won almost 50 caps, awaits the outcome of his trial for alleged match-fixing in a British court while Coventry's Ndlovu, Zimbabwe's most talented export, is holding out for a better package from his country's football association. He has not played for Zimbabwe for almost two years.

But the coach still thinks there is a place in Burkina Faso for the team. "We are in a good position and we have been preparing well," he said. ''These boys are on the right road, there's no doubt about that."
